analysis.one_liner: Tacks a 40 percent surtax onto the windfall profits of large oil companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 1991 and died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Gulf War oil price spike, this bill would have imposed an extra 40 percent tax on the profits large oil companies earned above their average profits over the previous five years. It applied to the biggest oil companies and to foreign owners with significant US oil operations. The money would have gone to the Treasury. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal Treasury would have collected 40 percent of the profits major oil companies earned above their recent five-year average, money available for public purposes or deficit reduction. Taxpayers generally benefit from that revenue. Consumers would have benefited only indirectly, unless Congress chose to spend the proceeds on them.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional tax equal to 40 percent of a large oil company's excess net profits — the amount its net income exceeds its average annual net income over the prior five years.

Targets only the biggest players: companies classified as major energy-producing firms that account for at least 1 percent of US oil or gas production, reserves, refining capacity, or petroleum product sales.
Also applies the same 40 percent excess-profits tax to foreign persons with US oil operations of at least 1 percent of the national total, so foreign-owned companies could not escape it.
Includes anti-avoidance rules directing the Treasury to write regulations preventing companies from dodging the tax through related parties and controlled corporate groups.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies, domestic and foreign, would have paid the tax on profits above their historical baseline. Those companies might have attempted to pass some of the cost through to consumers at the pump, and the tax could have modestly discouraged new investment in domestic oil production.

drawbacks.text: An excess profits tax on oil can be passed through to consumers in higher gasoline prices, which would leave ordinary drivers paying part of the bill — the chief lesson critics drew from the earlier windfall profits tax of 1980.

Because the tax is calculated off financial-statement net income over a fixed base period, it penalizes companies for unusually profitable years regardless of whether those profits came from windfall market conditions or from new investment, which could discourage domestic oil production and exploration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a straightforward windfall-profits recapture aimed at a concentrated industry during a wartime price spike, and its design (a five-year rolling baseline, tax computed off audited financial statements) was workable but blunt. The honest cost is the risk of pass-through to gasoline prices and some chilling of domestic oil investment. On balance it would have shifted money from a small set of very profitable companies to the general Treasury, with no offsetting benefit guaranteed to consumers unless Congress directed the revenue that way.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Excess Oil Profits Tax Act of 1991 on February 5, 1991, during the Gulf War, when oil prices had spiked.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.

The bill would have imposed a 40 percent tax on large oil companies' excess net profits — profits above their average over the prior five years — and applied the same tax to foreign owners with significant US oil operations.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies were better off: the wartime windfall profits they earned during the Gulf War price spike went untaxed, and the Treasury collected nothing from the bill. The Senate Finance Committee leadership avoided a fight over an oil tax it never scheduled.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Excess Oil Profits Tax Act of 1991 and lined up three cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Sen. William Cohen
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original Republican cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Three cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan group of supporters.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Chairman Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat for nearly two years and died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (2 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor), but with only three cosponsors in a 100-member Senate it never generated a floor fight; opposition took the form of committee inaction rather than recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 40 percent of their profits above a five-year baseline, directly cutting into the windfall earnings big oil companies enjoyed during the Gulf War price spike. Their interest in killing it ran against the Treasury's and, indirectly, taxpayers'.

industries.industry: Foreign-owned oil companies with US operations
industries.note: The same 40 percent excess-profits tax applied to foreign persons whose US production, reserves, refining capacity, or sales were at least 1 percent of the national total, closing off an ownership loophole.
